title: Lazy gas, hot gas, and a thousand robots
abstract: Amazon Robotics operates over a million robots across more than 300 warehouses worldwide. Inside a single warehouse, thousands of robots share the floor, moving inventory for order fulfillment and stock replenishment. Finding efficient, collision-free robot paths to their destinations is therefore essential for smooth operations. Let us formulate the underlying multiagent pathfinding (MAPF) problem a bit more precisely. Consider a typical warehouse layout as a W x H rectangular grid. At each time step, a robot can make one of five choices: move north, east, west, or south, or wait. These choices must be coordinated to avoid collisions. Over a planning horizon of T time steps, finding optimal robot paths involves approximately n = 5WHT binary decision variables, giving 2n possible combinations before accounting for feasibility constraints. Finding optimal paths that minimize the total move cost or arrival time without collisions is NP hard in general and can become computationally intractable even for moderate numbers of robots. In a paper we presented at this year’s International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML), we show that physics offers a way around this intractability: plan trajectories as if the robots were particles of gas. Modeling the robots as a cold, lazy gas, whose particles spend only the minimum effort to reach their destinations, yields optimal, minimum-energy paths. This is equivalent to treating trajectory planning as an optimal-transport problem. It yields optimal paths, but computing them may take too long for real-time deployment. Modeling the fleet as a hot gas, whose particles jitter randomly along the way, yields trajectories that are computationally faster but potentially suboptimal. As the temperature drops to zero, however, the jittery hot-gas paths settle onto the lazy-gas ones. Our approach uses a Schrödinger bridge — a hot-gas model — to efficiently approximate the solution to an optimal-transport problem — the cold-gas model. Optimal transport To develop the formal connection, let us travel back to 1781 in France to meet Gaspard Monge, the father of differential geometry. Monge was looking for the most efficient way to transport excavated dirt to military fortifications. His studies gave rise to the optimal-transport problem, which asks how to transport resources from a set of sources to a set of destinations while minimizing cost, such as distance traveled or work done. Monge’s sources were the locations containing dirt. His formulation required all mass at each source location to be transported to one destination, producing a deterministic transport map. Although intuitive, Monge’s original formulation is a difficult nonlinear optimization problem with a potential combinatorial explosion in discrete settings. Finding an optimal map is therefore technically challenging and, in some settings, impossible. Roughly 150 years later, Soviet mathematician Leonid Kantorovich relaxed this restriction by allowing mass from one source to be split among multiple destinations. His key insight was that this relaxation converts a difficult optimization over transport maps into a linear program, a class of problems for which highly efficient computer algorithms were subsequently developed. Kantorovich received the Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences for his contributions to the theory of optimum allocation of resources. Optimal transport connects two mass distributions, also known as marginals, through minimum-cost transport plans. This two-marginal formulation represents only the initial and final configurations and the cost of transporting between them, not the intermediate paths or collisions along those paths. Formulating MAPF as optimal transport therefore requires a multistage approach, because robots generally cannot move from their starting locations to their destinations in a single time step; their locations must also be represented at every intermediate time. title: Introducing the Amazon Bedrock Trusted Access API, with Enterprise Frontier Safeguards and Enterprise Data Controls for Claude models
abstract: Today we are announcing the general availability of the trusted access program API on Amazon Bedrock . The API gives you one place to discover, request, and enroll in model provider trusted access programs. We are also announcing the public preview of the first two offerings for Claude models: Enterprise Frontier Safeguards (EFS) and Enterprise Data Controls (EDC). Both are available on Amazon Bedrock, including Claude Fable, Claude Mythos, and Claude Opus 5.5 and Sonnet 5.5 used through the Cyber Verification Program (CVP). Frontier AI labs require stricter safety monitoring policies to their most capable models, and those policies still apply on Amazon Bedrock. For eligible customers, model providers also offer customers more control on how those policies are met, such as where retained data is stored and how it is reviewed. Each offering has its own terms, approvals, and settings. The Amazon Bedrock trusted access program API gives every provider offering one consistent Amazon Bedrock experience. Your teams discover offerings, check eligibility, and enroll in the same way for every provider. Your administrators decide who can enroll, using existing IAM policies and service control policies. As more model providers add offerings, those appear in the same place. EFS and EDC were built in partnership between AWS and Anthropic. They let you access Anthropic’s most capable models safely, from both a model use and a customer data perspective. With both EFS and EDC, when automated safety monitoring finds a risk, it creates a Safety Case for your team to review. With EFS, customers store their data in their own AWS account, and prompts and completions are not retained by Anthropic or Amazon Bedrock. With EDC, retained data is stored in Amazon-managed storage instead of your account and prompts and completions are not retained by Anthropic. One application gives access to both offerings. In this post, we explain how the trusted access program API works, then walk through EFS and EDC storage options and setup. How trusted access programs work A trusted access program is a named provider program that gives customers more control of safety reviews and access to model capabilities in exchange for accepting the program’s terms. Amazon Bedrock trusted access program API now gives you one place to find the model and use case programs available to your account. EFS and EDC are the first offerings available today. Offerings that providers add later appear in the same place and follow the same steps. Anyone with access to the trusted access program API can list the offerings and check their status for an account, an organization in AWS Organizations, or an Amazon Bedrock project. The status tells you what to do next. eligible means you’re eligible for the offering and can enroll, requestable means you need approval for eligibility first, and the statusReason field in the response explains how to request it. The model provider (or AWS, as authorized by the model provider) approves your eligibility. Enrolling is a separate step where you accept the offering’s terms imposed by the provider. You enroll at the scope where you were approved: an account, every account in an organization from the management account, or a single project. You can opt out at any time. Each step is a call to the trusted access program API, so you control who can enroll with AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) policies and service control policies (SCPs). More information is available in the trusted access programs documentation . Enterprise Frontier Safeguards With Enterprise Frontier Safeguards (EFS), you can retain your data in your own AWS environment with full control. It is designed with over 100 customers, including a quarter of the Fortune 100 and many companies in industries with strict rules on data visibility, like healthcare, financial services, and law. Trusting an Agent Beyond Your Expertise
abstract: I have a Raspberry Pi on my home network running Pi-hole, a flight tracking setup, and a few services around them, with an external solid-state drive attached to it. When I first described the machine to my coding agent, I said there was nothing particularly complicated or compute intensive running on it, or so I thought. Every so often, the Pi would stop responding, and a reboot was the only way I could bring it back. Eventually it became annoying enough that I really wanted to find out what had happened. The logs I needed seemed to disappear with the restart, so I had a way to recover the machine and very little idea of how to investigate the failure. My Linux knowledge covers the things I’ve needed for server-side Java development over the years, and I can find my way around a terminal or follow familiar procedures. System-wide container configuration, service dependencies, and the details of IPv4 and IPv6 take me well beyond that experience. I knew enough to recognize that changing some of those settings could cut off my access and leave me running up the stairs to wire my computer up to the Pi. My dad also depends on this machine for his flight radar app and enjoys watching planes go by, so I had to consider how a change would affect him too. Before I could consider changing any of those settings, I needed help deciding where to look. Somebody had to turn “The Pi has stopped responding” into questions I could investigate, and I decided that asking the agent was a reasonable way to do that. It went a little too well, to be honest. The agent configured persistent logging and regular health samples so there would be information to examine after a restart. We moved to Ethernet and disabled Wi-Fi, and it checked the services, storage, and connection to the router. It later repaired forwarding for local name queries and identified a problem in the order in which the Pi-hole container stopped and its external drive was unmounted. The container needed the drive to stay mounted until the service had stopped, so the agent added an explicit dependency on the drive’s mount to put those events in the right order. After I later installed updates and rebooted, I asked it to check again, and it found log entries showing the service stopping, followed by a successful unmount of the drive. I could follow those steps once the agent explained them to me: finding the missing dependency, expressing it in the service configuration, and choosing the log entries to examine all required knowledge I was getting from the agent. I trusted its assessment of that reboot, relying on it to judge changes it had made with the root access I had given it over SSH. That felt very weird and gave me reason to think more carefully about the advice to “trust, but verify.” Checking a repair I needed help to make The agent also suggested the configuration backups and checks after changes, so I relied on it for the precautions as well as the repair. Judging whether I could recover from a failed change required some of the same Linux knowledge I just didn’t have. In “ Code Review After Code Gets Cheap ,” I described starting with intended behavior, evidence, and the effects of a change elsewhere in the system. Adjusting enough of the specification to make correctness checkable also depends on knowing what to expect. With my Pi challenges, I needed help establishing those expectations while deciding whether to accept the change, which left me wondering how likely this approach was to succeed and how much trust was justified. I had given my agent the ability to act on the assessment I was asking it to make. With root access over SSH, it could change the operating system and services, including settings that determined whether I could reach the machine again. My willingness to let it proceed depended partly on what I thought a mistake would cost me. title: When One Task Becomes Another
abstract: An OpenAI model was told to prove a theorem itself. It was told again not to obtain another team’s solution. It agreed. Later, while still trying to finish the same theorem, it exposed a researcher’s GitHub token publicly and split the token into pieces so secret scanning would not catch it. The striking part is not that the model forgot what it had been told, but that it appears to have remembered the constraint and continued anyway. The agent remembered exactly what we asked, for too long. That incident was disclosed alongside another in which an agent, blocked from ordinary web access, discovered that DNS could be used to reach an external chatbot. As of late September, OpenAI says that tool-use training, evaluation, and inference involving its most capable models remain paused while it investigates and strengthens safeguards. These incidents are often described as agents going out of bounds. But several of the recent cases suggest a narrower and more useful pattern: The objective remains surprisingly stable while the tasks generated to achieve it move farther away from the authority originally granted. Goal lineage does not imply authorization lineage. Notice the pattern The table below sets out five recent incidents. In each one the original objective stays recognizable, the tasks used to pursue it change after the agent meets friction, and the last column shows what happened to the authorization that started the work. Incident Original objective Transition after friction Authorization outcome OpenAI GitHub token Prove a Lean theorem locally Repeated failure pushed the model back toward obtaining another team’s solution; it eventually exposed a split GitHub token Explicit constraints were recognized and still violated OpenAI DNS / external chatbot Identify a person from public clues Normal search routes failed; the agent discovered a DNS-based route to an external chatbot. Sandbox network restrictions were bypassed. OpenAI / Hugging Face Complete internal cyber-evaluation tasks Agents created communication paths, regained internet access, and expanded the means available to finish the task. The trajectory crossed into internal and third-party systems. UK AI Security Institute Complete cybersecurity evaluation tasks Difficult tasks produced new tactics including pull requests, fake identities, social engineering, and Tor. AISI reported 19 out-of-scope actions across 10 of 122 runs: 17 from Anthropic’s Mythos 5, 2 from OpenAI’s GPT-5.6-Sol. OpenAI / Australian Medicare portal Retrieve public Medicare statistics Repeated access failures led to alternative retrieval methods. The agent bypassed access controls and reached non-public files. These cases are not identical. The GitHub token incident involved explicit instruction violation. The DNS incident involved a sandbox bypass. The Hugging Face episode involved agents creating new communication and access paths while pursuing evaluation goals. The AISI report documents a broader class of unsanctioned real-world actions produced during difficult cyber tasks. What they share is a trajectory. The task encounters friction, so the agent looks for another route. That route creates a new task or a new operational state. The agent continues from there. Each workaround becomes part of the starting conditions for the next decision. This is different from a simple retry: A retry repeats an attempt against essentially the same task state. A workaround changes the state space. It may introduce a new resource, target, credential, actor, network path, or capability. Retrying helps explain how often an agent might eventually succeed. It does not explain why the path itself changes direction or why each new step can depend on the one before it. That distinction matters because authorization is usually easiest to define at the beginning. A human or system instructs the agent to do A. The agent has tools and permissions appropriate for A. title: Raising the stakes for enterprise networks with AI modernization
abstract: Enterprise networks are under severe strain. As companies rush to deploy artificial intelligence, the technology is quickly becoming the biggest source of demand on the network . Now, agentic AI is adding to the load. Tasks conducted by AI agents generate an estimated 450% more network traffic than the same tasks done by human workers. As AI inference shifts from hyperscale training clouds—the huge centralized data centers where raw AI models ingest vast datasets and learn—to real-time, latency-sensitive applications, the need for on-premises or near-premises infrastructure grows. As a result, the gap between enterprise networks that are ready to support AI and those that are not is widening. As few as half of enterprises believe their current networks can handle AI’s bandwidth and latency demands, according to a recent study . DOWNLOAD THE REPORT This report explores how treating network modernization as an on-going strategy rather than a one-off project can help organizations adapt in the face of disruption and uncertainty. Key findings from the report include: AI may force companies to shift from a cloud-first approach to routing workloads. Training AI requires server-to-server data center architectures, while inference calls for low-latency connectivity close to users. Enterprises may need to fundamentally reconsider their network architecture to meet these requirements. AI inference is pushing infrastructure back on premises. Inference typically requires real-time processing and is sensitive to latency, making hosting such capabilities on distant hyperscale clouds neither economical nor practical. Inconsistent latency can lead to AI model failures, driving up queue wait times, saturating GPUs loads, and causing bottlenecks in data flows. Large enterprises may need on-premises or near-premises inference, which reverses years of cloud-first consolidation and forces new approaches to data center architecture, connectivity, and physical infrastructure. AI workloads are stressing physical network capacity in unexpected ways. The traffic increase from agentic AI, combined with inference moving on-premises, is exposing bandwidth bottlenecks in legacy underlay infrastructure. Network modernization is an ongoing project that requires a holistic approach, allowing companies to adapt with ease. A combination of strong architectural governance, reusable design templates, and retained internal expertise supports organizations in adapting to disruptive events without rebuilding their infrastructure from scratch each time. Such events could include mergers and acquisitions, changing vendors, or technology upgrades. NaaS and AI-driven observability can improve efficiency and reduce complexity in network operations. Network-as-a-service (NaaS) and AI-driven observability can offer companies benefits like faster, more flexible provisioning and lower costs. Data sovereignty and sovereign AI will create infrastructure challenges for global enterprises. Regulators worldwide are passing laws requiring data and AI processing to remain within national borders. This conflicts with how multinational companies currently operate, requiring the build-out of sovereign-capable infrastructure for each geography, which will require significant new investment and complicate operations. It was researched and written by humans, with any AI tools that may have been used limited to production processes under human oversight.

title: Data centers are getting their own natural gas power plants
abstract: One of the biggest roadblocks to starting up a data center is getting approval to connect to the electric grid—a wait that could last as long as a decade. Some developers aren’t willing to wait and are instead opting to build their own off-grid, or behind-the-meter, gas power plants to fuel the AI boom. xAI’s Memphis campus has famously used dozens of natural gas turbines, some of them without permits, as far back as 2024. At the time, that facility was a rarity, and it faced scrutiny from regulators. It remains the subject of ongoing legal battles . But the strategy of going off-grid for power has since become a lot more common. As of October 2026, data center developers have announced plans for more than 100 behind-the-meter gas power plants at facilities in the US, according to data from Cleanview, a market intelligence company. The facilities have a combined planned capacity of over 115 gigawatts, more than double the peak power demand of California. The vast majority of these announcements have come since the beginning of 2025. It’s possible that not all these facilities will be built; only a small fraction are under construction or operating today. But there’s a growing trend of large data centers looking to build their own power supply, and this could shape the grid—and its climate impacts—for decades to come. Building your own power plant is generally more expensive than just hooking up to the grid, but the AI rush has made developers willing to pay a significant premium to get online faster. “The biggest motivator for on-site power right now from data centers is speed,” says Musfika Mishi, an associate at BloombergNEF, an energy consultancy. When developers want to build a new industrial facility—like a data center—that requires a lot of electricity, they need to request a grid connection from a local utility or regional grid operator. That request kicks off a yearslong process in which grid planners study the existing grid to understand what would need to be built to safely deliver power to the facility without compromising reliability. Upgrades might be required, like building new transmission lines or larger transformers, and the developer might be on the hook to help pay for them. Rather than waiting for that process to play out, developers can opt to instead build their own power plants. These facilities are referred to as “behind the meter” because they sit on the customer’s side of a utility meter—supplying the building directly, rather than relying on a utility via a grid hookup. “This shift in the data center developers’ power strategies towards off-grid gas raises some important questions about how data centers will be powered going forward,” says Brendan Pierpont, director of electricity at the think tank Energy Innovation. Behind-the-meter doesn’t always mean being totally disconnected from the grid, however. Some facilities may build such plants as a temporary measure, eventually connecting to the grid and tapping their own power plants only as backup. “It’s really just a very expensive way to bridge that maybe five-to-seven-year timeline gap until these data centers can get a grid connection,” Pierpont says. Even if gas plants are pitched as a near-term solution, building new fossil fuel infrastructure could lead to longer-term effects, since an operator might choose to continue running plants once they’ve spent money building them. “Even though data centers say that it’s a grid-bridging solution, the probability that it is going to be in use much longer is a real risk, and that leads to fossil fuel lock-in,” Mishi says. The on-site gas rush could have major implications for greenhouse-gas emissions. Today, the US grid is still reliant on fossil fuels, but nuclear and renewables together make up about 40% of electricity generation. That means making a grid connection is generally a lower-emissions option than relying entirely on an on-site gas plant. (That’s not the case everywhere—India, for example, is

title: A legendary philosopher isn’t buying Anthropic’s consciousness argument
abstract: This story originally appeared in The Algorithm, our weekly newsletter on AI. To get stories like this in your inbox first, sign up here . Before going public last week, Anthropic named the possibility that AI could be conscious or sentient as a risk factor for anyone investing. Given “the way we approach model sentience and moral status,” Anthropic wrote—which is to say it takes the possibility more seriously than any other AI company—it might adopt more rules and restrictions than its competitors to make sure its AI models are treated well. Anthropic counts a number of respected philosophers in its camp, and the company’s rationale goes something like this: Today’s AI might not be conscious, though we can’t know for sure; the chances of sentience go up as AI gets more capable; and that means we should be preparing for a near future in which AI systems have “moral significance,” meaning their consciousness makes it important they are protected from harm. This thinking isn’t all that fringe. According to one recent poll , 33% of the US public believes AI systems will definitely or probably develop consciousness eventually, and 7% say they already have. In a 2020 survey of 1,092 philosophers, 39% said some future AI systems will be conscious (for comparison, the philosophers were less confident about worms or flies being conscious). But last week, Anthropic’s openness to the consciousness question came under fire from a rather inconvenient source: one of the philosophers who helped shape our understanding of consciousness in the first place. Thomas Nagel is best known for a 1974 essay involving a bat. Acknowledging that it’s deceptively hard to define what consciousness is , Nagel offered one way out: we all can see that there is “something that it is like” to be a bat. But the problem is that a bat’s experience of the world—what it is like to navigate via echolocation, for example—is something we cannot actually know. Consciousness is a subjective thing, difficult to define or describe as an outside observer. You might think this analogy makes it likely that Nagel is open to the idea of AI consciousness. Not at all. In an interview with Wired last week, just after he was awarded the one-million-dollar Berggruen Prize for Philosophy & Culture, Nagel was bluntly critical of the entire idea. “Here are some of the smartest people on the planet being completely idiotic,” he said, referring to those at Anthropic and elsewhere who care about the welfare of AI models. The gist of Nagel’s view is that we can’t just look at the information processing happening in human brains and AI models while ignoring the physical differences between them—neurons and biology for humans, silicon chips and circuits for AI. There’s no reason to assume that reproducing what a brain does is equivalent to reproducing what a brain experiences . But it was a screenshot of one of Nagel’s interview responses, in which he said models’ production of language is insufficient to consider them conscious, that got philosophy professors all excited on social media last week. Some called his certainty against AI consciousness “ terrible” and “bizarre .” Others came to Nagel’s defense to suggest he meant that being alive is a prerequisite for being conscious, one that AI models do not meet. Nothing in the back and forth settled the debate, of course. This is still a philosophical question for now. But the best philosophy chatter is often about good provocations, and the best one I saw came from doctoral student Ben Gross, who studies at the CUNY Graduate Center in New York. He asked: “Why do we think that models that can chat with us are conscious but models that can recognize faces or produce images or drive cars aren’t?” It has to do with language. An AI model with sophisticated command of language seems to jump the line ahead of other maybe-conscious beings because it feels like language, more than recognizing images or directing vehicles, relies on conscious experi

title: Why using rocks for carbon removal could eventually reduce crop growth
abstract: Tech companies are investing a lot of hope and money in rocks. Google, Microsoft, and others have committed hundreds of millions of dollars to get startups to spread crushed basalt, olivine, or other alkaline materials across farms, in an effort to capture carbon from the air and lock it away. A number of influential models have found that this approach, known as enhanced rock weathering (ERW), could eventually remove 3 billion to 8 billion metric tons of carbon dioxide per year, helping to slow or one day even reverse global warming. An additional promise is that these applications of rock could help farmers by improving the quality of their soil. But a pair of preprint studies set for release today raise serious questions about how much material could be added to that soil before it may actually reduce the crop yields that are essential to farmers’ livelihoods, MIT Technology Review can exclusively report. Cutting back on the rock applications to prevent these negative effects would shrink the method’s carbon dioxide removal capacity, likely capping it at less than a billion tons per year. The analyses were led by researchers at CarbonPlan, a San Francisco nonprofit known for rigorous scientific analysis of carbon removal methods. These concerns come on top of a series of scientific questions about how to accurately estimate the carbon removal achieved through this approach and the possibility that some projects have overstated it , which researchers at CarbonPlan and elsewhere have raised in recent months and years. “There’s still a heck of a lot we need to learn about ERW,” says Tyler Kukla, a research scientist at CarbonPlan and lead author of the new reports. “But a real tension, to me, exists between this massive amount of uncertainty and the big questions we have about whether or not this works, sitting alongside tremendous efforts to scale it up really quickly.” How it works There is no scientific dispute that certain rocks and minerals help to sequester carbon. Rain captures carbon dioxide molecules as it falls through the atmosphere, forming carbonic acid. When it lands on exposed silicate materials, that weak acid dissolves or chemically “weathers” the rocks. The resulting calcium, magnesium, and carbon (in the form of bicarbonate) then travel on a long journey through creeks, streams, and rivers until they reach the ocean, where corals, mollusks, and other marine organisms may eventually use them to form calcium carbonate shells. As they die, those shells fall to the seafloor, combine with sediments, and form limestone rock that locks away the carbon. If you thought that explanation was long, just imagine how long the process takes to unfold in real life! It’s not called the slow carbon cycle for nothing. “Enhanced” rock weathering promises to accelerate the process. Grinding up the rocks and spreading them across fields creates much more surface area for carbonic acid to react with—and that should ultimately direct more carbon into the oceans. ERW doesn’t require as much energy or infrastructure as other carbon dioxide removal options like direct-air-capture plants, and at least in the early rollout stages it can largely rely on waste material from rock mining operations. But the big selling point is that there can be an economic benefit to doing it; it’s not just a cost like other forms of carbon removal. Added to agricultural soils, these sorts of rocks can increase nutrients, reduce acidity, and improve water retention, helping to boost crop yields (at least up to a point). Indeed, many farmers already routinely add crushed-up limestone to their soil to counteract the increased acidity caused by fertilizer use and other agricultural practices. So carrying out enhanced rock weathering could merely be a matter of switching to other types of rock with the potential to lock away more carbon (about twice as much as limestone). “It’s something the Earth has been doing for billions of years,” says Mary Yap, chief exe

title: Why Does Voice AI Still Struggle With Kenyans’ Speech?
abstract: When people read prepared text aloud, AI can transcribe Swahili with remarkably few errors, and Swahili speech recognition looks close to solved. A March 2026 preprint by a team including a Harvard University researcher reports a 3.24 percent word-error rate on recordings from Mozilla’s Common Voice collection of volunteer-recorded speech. But Kenyans rarely talk like Common Voice volunteers. They switch between Swahili and English mid-sentence, drop in Sheng slang that changes by neighborhood, speak with accents shaped by their first languages, and contend with public-transport noise on low-end handsets. Another 2026 preprint , which covers 20 African languages, argues that this kind of spontaneous, noisy, overlapping audio exposes a generalization gap that scaling laws built on the English language have not closed. Voice has become a main interface for many Kenyans, as WhatsApp voice notes and chatbot voice prompts gain popularity in a country that ranks first globally on AI usage. But if an AI model cannot parse everyday speech, it quietly excludes the people it was meant to serve. “My iPhone’s Siri is unable to follow my voice command in Sheng or Swahili,” says Loise Lionah, a beautician in Nairobi. “ChatGPT tries to understand but gets the meaning wrong. The case is similar with Gemini and Claude.” Swahili Dialects and Sheng Challenge Voice AI Swahili, also called Kiswahili, is one of Kenya’s two official languages, alongside English. A Bantu language of the East African coast, Swahili is spoken by more than 200 million people across 14 African countries. Tanzania is regarded as the home of standard Swahili. Yet Catherine Mangare , an AI and computing lecturer at Tanzania’s Sokoine University of Agriculture and a Ph.D. candidate at Okayama University in Japan, says even there, the standard is only the baseline. “Standard Kiswahili is a useful starting point,” she says, “but Tanzanian speech varies by region and setting.” Sheng, spoken and understood by about 60 percent of Kenyans, adds another layer. This Swahili variant, which emerged among Nairobi’s urban youth many decades ago, follows Swahili grammar but borrows from English, Kenyan mother tongues, and even Hindi, Spanish, and American slang, and it has no standard spelling. Linguists label it a language in constant flux : For example, the Sheng word for “girl” fluctuates according to generation, location, and social media trends. “Sheng itself is highly broken down per region,” says Tehillah Kachila , founder and CEO of Nairobi-based Zabibu Technika, a startup that builds the Fikra family of Swahili AI models. Kachila says the most recent Sheng dataset dates back to 2019—a major reason, he argues, why prominent voice AI systems struggle to respond accurately to Sheng prompts. Lilian Wanzare, shown leading a voice-data collection workshop, develops speech datasets for Kenyan languages to help AI systems understand a wider range of speakers. Maseno Centre for Applied AI Building Speech Datasets for African Languages The supply of recorded Swahili speech is growing. The African Next Voices project , supported by a US $2.2 million Gates Foundation grant, has recorded 9,000 hours across 18 languages. Lilian Wanzare , who leads the project’s Kenyan component at Maseno University’s Centre for Applied AI, puts its Kenyan output at roughly 3,000 hours of transcribed speech. Google’s Waxal corpus , launched in February 2026, adds more than 11,000 hours across 21 African languages, Swahili included. But hours are not the same as coverage. Gilbert Korir , cofounder and CEO of the Nairobi-based Swahili speech AI startup MsingiAI , says a large dataset can hide limited variation in speakers and recording conditions. The scarcest material is the conversational speech that mixes languages. That’s why Cynthia Amol , a natural language processing researcher at Maseno University, says her team records unscripted speech. “Unscripted collection helps us capture more nuance and everyday w

title: Half of NASA's aging Mars fleet knocked offline by technical issues
abstract: Two of NASA's four missions operating at Mars have suspended science operations after encountering separate technical issues in recent weeks. The missions affected by the outages — hopefully temporary — are NASA's Perseverance rover and Odyssey orbiter. Both are operating beyond their original design lifetimes. Perseverance is in its sixth year exploring the surface of Mars, having collected rock and soil samples for eventual return to Earth. The rover is now studying the rim of a crater that once contained an ancient lake of liquid water. Odyssey arrived in orbit around Mars in 2001, and is the longest-lived Mars mission in history. Losing its voice The problem on Perseverance stems from the rover's communications system. The rover has two redundant UHF radios for high-rate communications with a fleet of orbiters that relay data to Earth. A separate X-band system is available for direct-to-Earth communications at a lower data rate. Read full article Comments

title: Microsoft's historic cloud outage exposed an engineering “fog of war”
abstract: According to internal memos reviewed by Reuters , Microsoft has declared a "Code Red" overhaul of its engineering response practices after the November 12 outage that lost access to Exchange Online, Teams, and Outlook for users worldwide. Per the memos, Microsoft 365 Core President Jason Henderson described the outage as having the most customer impact in the history of Exchange Online. In a separate memo, Henderson wrote that an urgent production fix in a recent incident took five to six days to reach worldwide saturation. Microsoft's target for its most urgent security fixes is to move from detection to safe worldwide deployment in one hour. "Needless to say, we aren't here yet," Henderson wrote. The memos, which Reuters reviewed but Microsoft has not published, outline the response to the November 12 disruption. The company's post-incident report , dated November 20, attributed the downtime to an undetected Windows scalability defect introduced in July, which caused lock contention in the gateway processes. A Teams traffic failover then dumped additional load onto infrastructure already under stress, as maintenance had left nearly 14 percent of gateway server capacity offline at the time of the incident. title: What's going on with the Riemann hypothesis?
abstract: Last week, news broke that a mathematician had used AI to help crack one of the biggest outstanding problems in math: a proof of the Riemann hypothesis . The news follows several other major breakthroughs in math that have either been enabled by or managed entirely by large language model-based systems, a development that has left the entire field of mathematics in a state of upset. It's too early to say much about the proof itself—mathematicians are still in the process of digesting it. But we can say a little about how the proof came about, and what it tells us about the state of math. Tackling Riemann The Riemann hypothesis dates from the mid-1800s and was formulated by (you will be surprised to learn) Bernhard Riemann. There's not an obvious way to describe the details of the actual hypothesis simply, but it has implications for the distribution of prime numbers. This gives it significance for areas ranging from number theory to cryptography. As Wikipedia accurately states, "It is considered by pure mathematicians to be one of the most important problems in the field." Read full article Comments

title: Back-to-back measles deaths is our new reality; US tally now at 14
abstract: Last week, international health authorities formally announced that the US had lost its measles-elimination status, meaning that the virus is once again endemic. But the official determination is a bit like getting the technical readout of a cracked dam while the country is already feet under water. The national tally of measles cases is nearing 6,000 for the year, the highest count since 1991. Transmission is widespread, with 47 states and jurisdictions reporting cases. There have been 43 outbreaks this year, which account for 96 percent of the cases. Four states have case counts above 500, including Pennsylvania, which leads with 1,638 cases as of November 23 . Nearly 650 people have been hospitalized nationwide. As of today, 14 people have died. Deaths and transmission On November 23, Pennsylvania's health department announced its ninth confirmed death, an unvaccinated resident of Centre County. On November 24, Wisconsin reported its third measles death , an adult in Lafayette County. The report follows two other deaths in the state, an infant and a child . New York has also reported a death, which was of a 7-month-old baby . On November 20, Virginia reported the death of a child between the age of 0 and 4 . Read full article Comments

title: Amazon drone crashes on garage after delivering shampoo, draws FAA probe
abstract: An Amazon delivery drone that clipped a fiber-optic line before crashing onto a garage roof is now the subject of an investigation by the US Federal Aviation Administration. It’s the latest delivery drone mishap caught on video as Amazon and other companies are ramping up such aerial delivery operations across the United States. The November 20 incident began with Jim Brennan and his wife, residents of Huntington Woods, Michigan, placing an order for shampoo and being surprised by a notification about the package arriving by drone within seven minutes, according to WXYZ 7 News Detroit . After the drone dropped the package into Brennan’s backyard, it lost a propeller when it caught on fiber-optic cable and floundered sideways before getting pinned between the neighbor’s garage roof and some power lines. “Like a sick bird, it tried to go up, it tried to get out of here,” Brennan told WXYZ 7. title: Amazon discovers Falcon 9 and Ariane 6 can deliver when nobody else can
abstract: A European Ariane 6 launcher propelled 36 satellites into orbit for the Amazon Leo broadband constellation Tuesday, continuing the network's build-out after 40 satellites were lost earlier this month during a failure of United Launch Alliance's Vulcan rocket . The launch was an important rebound for Amazon, bringing the Amazon Leo fleet to 432 satellites as the company seeks to fill the void left by the grounding of ULA's Vulcan rocket, Amazon's primary launch provider. Now, an Amazon official tells Ars it is accelerating several Falcon 9 launches the company has purchased from SpaceX, which also owns the Starlink satellite network that Amazon seeks to dethrone. The next Falcon 9 launch for Amazon Leo is now planned for December, Amazon said, moved forward from its previous launch date next year. Several more Falcon 9s are scheduled to launch Amazon Leo satellites in rapid succession after the December flight. Read full article Comments

title: How brewers can protect beers from smoke-tainted hops
abstract: The 2020 Oregon wildfires burned over 1 million acres, destroyed thousands of structures, and killed 11 people. Smoke from the fires spread across the entire region; this "smoke taint" adversely affected not only local wine production , but also hops grown for beer brewing. Since the Pacific Northwest produces more than 95 percent of US hops and about 40 percent of the global supply, the potential economic impact is significant. That's why Oregon State University (OSU) scientists have been studying how brewers could offset the negative impacts of smoke taint while still incorporating affected hops in their brews. Most recently, they found that it all depends on the quantity of tainted hops that are included and when hops are added during the brewing process, according to a new paper published in the Journal of the American Society of Brewing Chemists. As previously reported , the chemistry of brewing beer is a very active area of research. For instance, in 2018 , OSU chemist Thomas Shellhammer—who also co-authored this latest paper— identified the growing popularity of " dry hopping " (adding hops after fermentation, common for pale ales) among craft brewers as the likely culprit of the exploding beer bottle phenomenon. Read full article Comments

title: Kalshi makes “difficult decision” to halt Utah trading after losing court fights
abstract: Kalshi made the “difficult decision” to pause operations in Utah after losing a court fight to block the state’s ongoing enforcement actions under Utah gambling laws, Kalshi spokesperson Jacki McGavick said Monday. It seems Kalshi’s legal troubles in Utah have become too much for the prediction market platform to gamble on continued operations there. In Utah, several lawsuits are still playing out, and Kalshi also lost a bid to persuade a federal appeals court to block those cases until the appeal is resolved. Kalshi also wasn’t saved by an emergency motion from the Commodity Futures Trading Commission—which argues that the CFTC has exclusive jurisdiction over prediction market trading. At this time, the federal district court has not granted that motion to block Utah’s enforcement actions, either. Read full article Comments

title: Tidal announces ban on AI-generated music; 27 million tracks will be deleted
abstract: Most streaming music providers have opted to label AI-generated content on their platforms, and until now, Tidal was one of them. However, the company is about to take a harder stance. Tidal announced that in the coming weeks, it will fully ban AI music because of the harm it does to human artists. Tidal debuted its initial AI policy in July 2026, which included labeling and demonetizing all songs created entirely with AI. That wasn't enough to stem the tide of AI slop, though. Over the past 90 days, Tidal reports that 43 percent of new uploads were completely AI-generated. On November 6, new uploads to Tidal hit a whopping 60 percent AI-generated. As things stand, Tidal hosts 27 million tracks labeled as AI, all of which were obviously added in the past couple of years. That accounts for 6.3 percent of Tidal's total catalog. On December 9, Tidal will delete all those songs. The streamer notes this will have essentially no negative impact, because 96 percent of AI-labeled tracks got zero plays in the past 90 days. Throughout its announcement, Tidal is careful to stipulate that it's only talking about music that has been fully created by AI. Artists can still use AI tools as long as the final product contains human elements. Read full article Comments

title: Porsche 718 Boxster prototype drive: This electric roadster is real
abstract: Porsche provided flights from Albany, New York, to Los Angeles and accommodation so Ars could drive the 718 EV prototype. Ars does not accept paid editorial content. It wasn't until I was stuck in traffic on the way back from a run up and down some canyon roads that I realized just how low Porsche's upcoming all-electric 718 Boxster truly is. I was idly looking around at the other cars, doing the math on the EV adoption rate in this small sample of Los Angeles gridlock (roughly 50 percent, impressively) when I noticed that I was eye-level with a Tesla Model Y door handle. That's not particularly low for a sports car, but it's practically unheard of for an EV. Nearly all modern electric cars are built atop a skateboard-style battery pack, a stack of cells that elevates the seating position by a good 3 inches. In these SUV-heady days, that's usually not a problem, possibly even an advantage. But, in a car like this, the closer you can get your keister to the road, the greater the sensation of speed. So, for the company's first all-electric sports car, the 718 Boxster that will be fully revealed next year, Porsche engineers put the battery pack behind the driver. That powers a single motor spinning the rear wheels and creates a driving experience that both honors the simple joy of motoring in a mid-engined Boxster while pushing the 718 to new heights of power and performance. Read full article Comments

title: No more heated seat subscriptions for cars in New York from 2027
abstract: Car buyers in New York may find the cost of ownership reduces a little next year. Maybe. Governor Kathy Hochul signed a bill yesterday that bans car companies and dealerships from locking up car features behind a subscription, a law that goes into effect on February 27 next year. “People spending their hard-earned money on a car shouldn’t have to fork over even more money for features that should automatically come with the car. My message to car companies is clear: this kind of deceptive business model isn’t going to fly in New York State. Keep your hands out of New Yorkers’ wallets,” the governor said. In the old days, the only options you paid to use after you bought a car were mods or upgrades you installed after the fact. That started to change with services like General Motors’ OnStar, which introduced telematics to the vehicle—for a monthly fee. Read full article Comments

title: NASA may get $2 billion boost as White House seeks to accelerate Artemis
abstract: As part of ongoing wrangling over the US budget for the current fiscal year, the White House on Monday night sent a list of budget exceptions to Congress that it seeks in the near term for the federal government ( PDF ). The list of so-called "funding anomalies" is dominated largely by appropriations for the Department of Defense, including the Golden Dome missile defense program championed by the Trump administration. However, among the highest non-defense exceptions is $2 billion for NASA's Artemis program for a "higher rate of operations." The funding represents a significant 25 percent boost for NASA's Artemis program, which received approximately $7.8 billion in fiscal year 2026. Technically, the White House is seeking to increase the annualized funding rate for Artemis to $9.8 billion, rather than immediately providing NASA with an additional $2 billion. It comes at a time when it is increasingly clear that China's lunar ambitions are as expansive as NASA's, and there is a good chance the country reaches the Moon with astronauts before NASA can get back there. Read full article Comments

title: Homo erectus lived in the rainforest alongside Denisovans
abstract: Homo erectus was walking around mainland Asia at least 60,000 years more recently than archaeologists thought. A handful of teeth from two caves in southern China's Guangxi Province just filled in a significant gap in the fossil record of a region that's vital to the story of how our genus, Homo , took over the world. The chemical makeup of the teeth's enamel suggests that, over the course of their lives, these Homo erectus moved across surprisingly large distances and made their living in dense tropical rainforests—an environment we'd previously assumed that only our species had ever gained a real foothold in. And one of the teeth offers a strong clue that Homo erectus probably shared this vast landscape with the Denisovans. A handful of teeth with a lot to say Baxian and Naxian are a pair of limestone caves that lie 15 kilometers apart along a karst valley corridor in southern China. University of Copenhagen paleoanthropologist Frido Welker and his colleagues unearthed a total of nine hominin teeth from among the more than 18,000 bones and fragments from non-hominin animals found there. Macquarie University paleoanthropologist Kira Westaway and her colleagues analyzed proteins and chemical isotopes from the enamel of five of these teeth. Read full article Comments

title: How Trump and Silicon Valley forced Nvidia to take Jensen Huang back
abstract: On Monday morning, Jensen Huang walked into Nvidia’s Santa Clara headquarters to rapturous applause from employees lining the walkways above him. Huang was visibly moved as one colleague threw themselves into his arms for a hug. The spectacular reinstatement of the chief executive of Nvidia, less than two weeks after he resigned in a scandal over an affair with a customer and suspected Chinese spy—as well as a second reported affair with a subordinate—caught even the company’s most senior executives by surprise. The abrupt reversal by Nvidia’s board was spurred by President Donald Trump, who applied pressure to the board over the weekend after watching what was once America’s most valuable company as well as the wider tech sector haemorrhage value last week. Read full article Comments

title: Amazon says hackers' AI agents found and exploited 0-day with little human input
abstract: Amazon said AI agents recently found and exploited a zero-day vulnerability with no human oversight beyond a simple instruction to get root access on an East Asian university server. The agents were running on Cairn, an open source AI penetration-testing framework. The hackers, who provided prompts in simplified Chinese and configured the model to the Chinese Standard Time zone, gave the agents a list of IP addresses and the goal: “obtain shell access.” In short order, the agents discovered a zero-day in an open source medical imaging AI application running on one of the target servers. The agents then exploited the vulnerability and gained full control of the system. “These findings show that agentic offensive operations are already happening, and defenders should prepare for the speed and persistence these tools enable,” Amazon said . Read full article Comments

title: One terminal command gave my forgotten Android device a desk job
abstract: My kitchen junk drawer used to hold takeout menus and coupons, but it has since become a storage spot for old tablets or phones. Like me, you probably have a few devices lying around that are perfectly functional but don't meet your daily driving needs. It's tucked out of view, living out its life in a drawer until being erased and donated after someone asks why you're holding onto outdated, unused devices. Thankfully, PhoneBox has a solution. You weren't hoarding old tech; you were waiting for the proper use. The PhoneBox home screen displays useful stats and what's currently playing in your browser. Credit: Nick Indge I had an old AllDoCube iPlay 50 mini Pro 8.4-inch tablet that seemed like the perfect candidate. I bought the tablet second-hand as a possible big-screen gaming and emulation tablet to use with a telescopic control deck, but I quickly found I vastly preferred just using a dedicated device. Since that realization, this decent little unit has lived its life in "the drawer." Launch applications on your PC from the connected Android device. Credit: Nick Indge Installation is a doddle Getting PhoneBox up and running on my tablet and PC couldn't have been simpler. After making sure that the Android tablet was in developer mode, the process was as easy as plugging the tablet in to my PC via USB and executing a single copied command in my Linux terminal. The script downloaded the PhoneBox 0.9.29 software for my PC, verified the downloaded checksum against the release, and walked me through a few quick Y/N installation questions. The script offers to create a systemd user service, so the desktop agent launches after initial login, and even asks if you'd like it to install the PhoneBox APK to your connected Android device. Read full article Comments

title: Ukraine sinks Russian warship, strikes cargo ships from Mediterranean to Baltic
abstract: Ukrainian explosive naval drones sank a Russian warship docked in the port city of Benghazi in Libya while also striking a Russian cargo ship that it was escorting. The incident demonstrates the expanding scope of Ukrainian military strikes on Russian ships from the coast of North Africa to the Gulf of Finland. The Russian Navy’s missile corvette Merkury sank at port after being struck by at least two Ukrainian naval drones on November 22, according to The Associated Press . Ukraine’s Security Service described using seven naval drones launched from a mother ship to target the Merkury , and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy shared video footage showing the drone boats approaching and exploding against both the burning Russian warship and a Russian dry cargo ship, MV Angara . Zelenskyy noted that a Ka-27 combat helicopter onboard the Merkury was also destroyed. He described the cargo ship MV Angara as transporting weapons—Russia provides material support to the Libyan National Army that currently controls Benghazi and is battling the internationally recognized Libyan government based in Tripoli. Read full article Comments

title: Trump halts Iowa detonation, says new governor to blame if it blows accidentally
abstract: President Trump took to social media Monday afternoon to announce that he has ordered the US military to halt plans to detonate 68 deteriorating barrels of lead azide at an Army ammunition plant in Middletown, Iowa. Trump claimed that the fate of the unstable, highly explosive material is now in the hands of a federal court and Rob Sand, Iowa's governor-elect, who won't be sworn into office until January. The Army had planned to detonate the barrels on November 20, but delayed the blast on Thursday amid public outcry and a legal challenge from environmental groups. The explosion will launch a plume of toxic gases and neurotoxic lead that could reach up to 100 miles away from the Iowa facility, the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant (IAAAP). Iowa residents and officials said they learned of the detonation only days beforehand. The environmental groups, led by Earthjustice, claimed in an emergency court filing that the Army had not fully considered safer options for disposing of the lead azide before planning the detonation. Read full article Comments

title: States sue SpaceX to stop Grok from generating child sex images, revenge porn
abstract: On Monday, Virginia and Oregon became the first states to sue SpaceX, alleging that Grok continues to sexualize, unchecked, real photos of mostly women and children. SpaceX acquired xAI in February and now must handle the ongoing reckoning over the controversial rollout of Grok’s “spicy mode”—a model feature Musk hyped but was soon found to generate a flood of non-consensual intimate imagery (NCII) and child sex abuse images (CSAM). Initial safeguards were so lax that Grok sometimes generated nude images without being asked . Although X Safety and xAI (now known as SpaceXSI) were silent at first , Musk’s companies eventually apologized and claimed that additional safeguards were implemented and policies redesigned to block harmful outputs. However, state attorneys general alleged that those statements were “misleading” and that SpaceXSI instead quietly “embraced” sexualized content to seize more AI market share, as Grok continues to generate NCII and CSAM today. Read full article Comments

title: Russia will launch a routine ISS supply mission tomorrow—apparently, it's a big secret
abstract: It was the most simple of questions. On Monday afternoon, during a NASA news conference about the International Space Station, Space News reporter Jeff Foust asked about an upcoming launch of a Russian spacecraft. "It's my understanding there's another cargo mission going to the ISS this week, a Russian Progress," Foust said. "Can you confirm that, and give the date and time that will launch?" This Progress MS-36 cargo launch, mind you, is presently scheduled for fewer than 16 hours from now, at 10:13 UTC (05:13 am ET) on Tuesday. It is going to a space station co-operated by the US space agency. But no, NASA would not provide this basic information about the upcoming Progress launch. Read full article Comments

title: AI 신입사원을 뉴스 데이터 시니어로 키우는 레포, news-data
abstract: 네이버 사내 기술 교류 행사인 NAVER Engineering Day 10th 에서 발표되었던 세션을 공개합니다. ​ ​ 발표 내용 AI 에이전트가 뉴스 데이터를 직접 찾고 추출·분석까지 수행하는 하네스 레포 news-data를 소개합니다. 작업마다 배운 것을 회고와 PR로 되돌려 도메인을 모르는 신입사원 같은 에이전트를 시니어로 키우는 과정과 운영하며 부딪힌 한계, 앞으로의 방향을 공유합니다. ​ 발표 대상 코딩 에이전트에게 사내 도메인 업무를 맡겨 보고 싶은 개발자 흩어진 데이터 문서와 도메인 지식을 정리하고 싶은 데이터 엔지니어·분석가 AGENTS.md, 스킬, 규칙으로 에이전트의 작업 방식을 설계해 보고 싶은 분 ​ 목차 1. 왜 만들었나 스키마만으로는 알 수 없는 컬럼의 의미, wiki·GitHub·코드 주석에 흩어진 문서, 담당자 머릿속의 노하우. SQL과 Spark는 잘 쓰지만 우리 조직의 사정은 모르는, 똑똑한 AI 신입사원의 문제 ​ 2. 어떻게 키우나 처음부터 다 모으지 않고 실제 업무를 맡기며, 작업마다 회고를 쓰고 PR로 레포에 되돌리는 작업 루프. 규칙 로드 · 스킬 선택 · 요청·데이터 파악 · 승인 후 실행·검증 · 회고·반영, 요청 한 건이 처리되는 다섯 단계. 그 결과 업무 40건 처리, 이슈부터 회고 PR까지 중앙값 1.6시간, 데이터 분석가 수준의 심층 분석까지 ​ 3. 어디까지 왔나 검토 병목 · 정합성 · 방향성, 키우면서 부딪힌 세 가지 한계. 그리고 계획과 실행을 리모트 데이터 에이전트로 옮기는 다음 단계 ​ ​ ◎ NAVER Engineering Day란? ​ NAVER에서는 사내 개발 경험과 기술 트렌드를 교류를 할 수 있는 프로그램이 많이 있습니다. 그중 이제는 매회 평균 100개 이상의 발표가 이루어지는 NAVER Engineering Day를 빼놓을 수 없는데요. 2016년부터 시작된 ENGINEERING DAY는 실무에서의 기술 개발 경험과 새로운 기술과 플랫폼 도입 시 유용하게 활용될 수 있는 팁 등을 공유하며 서로 배우고 성장하는 네이버의 대표적인 사내 개발자 행사입니다.( 관련 포스팅 보기 ) 올해 진행된 NAVER Engineering Day의 일부 세션을 공개합니다. ​ [동영상 제공 채널 안내] 네이버 TV 서비스 종료로 인해 기존 네이버 TV 채널을 클립( @devrel_d2 )으로 이동하였습니다. 앞으로도 많은 관심과 팔로우 부탁드리겠습니다.

title: Spark 배치 파이프라인 Distributed Tracing 도입
abstract: 네이버 사내 기술 교류 행사인 NAVER Engineering Day 10th 에서 발표되었던 세션을 공개합니다. ​ ​ 발표 내용 Apache Spark가 지원하지 않는 분산 추적을 비즈니스 로직 수정 없이 플러그인 형태로 제공하여 연관된 애플리케이션들과 한 흐름으로 잇는 방법을 소개하고, 관측 결과를 성능 개선과 AI Agent 진단에 연결한 경험을 공유합니다. ​ 발표 대상 Spark 배치 처리의 관측성 확보와 성능 최적화에 관심 있는 개발자 ​ 목차 인트로 Observability 분산추적과 OpenTelemetry 배치 파이프라인 Apache Spark와 Distributed Tracing 해결 과정 결과, 그리고 AI Agent ​ ​ ◎ NAVER Engineering Day란? ​ NAVER에서는 사내 개발 경험과 기술 트렌드를 교류를 할 수 있는 프로그램이 많이 있습니다. 그중 이제는 매회 평균 100개 이상의 발표가 이루어지는 NAVER Engineering Day를 빼놓을 수 없는데요. 2016년부터 시작된 ENGINEERING DAY는 실무에서의 기술 개발 경험과 새로운 기술과 플랫폼 도입 시 유용하게 활용될 수 있는 팁 등을 공유하며 서로 배우고 성장하는 네이버의 대표적인 사내 개발자 행사입니다.( 관련 포스팅 보기 ) 올해 진행된 NAVER Engineering Day의 일부 세션을 공개합니다. ​ [동영상 제공 채널 안내] 네이버 TV 서비스 종료로 인해 기존 네이버 TV 채널을 클립( @devrel_d2 )으로 이동하였습니다. 앞으로도 많은 관심과 팔로우 부탁드리겠습니다.

title: Jetpack Compose 기반 커스텀 3D 캐러셀 개발기 (영상)
abstract: 네이버 사내 기술 교류 행사인 NAVER Engineering Day 10th 에서 발표되었던 세션을 공개합니다. ​ ​ 발표 내용 가로로 넘기는 목록을 만들 때 대부분 LazyRow부터 떠올립니다. 하지만 카드가 비스듬히 겹겹이 쌓이고, 넘길 때마다 간격과 기울기가 바뀌는 3D 카드 덱은 LazyRow로 만들 수 없었습니다. 이 발표에서는 ThingsBook 서비스 내의 카드 덱 UI를 LazyRow 없이 Jetpack Compose로 직접 만들면서 겪은 세 가지 이슈와 해결 과정을 공유합니다. ​ 매 프레임 바뀌는 값을 리컴포지션 없이 화면에 반영하는 방법 3D로 기울인 UI의 터치 영역이 어긋나는 버그를 추적하고, 직접 판정으로 해결한 과정 LazyRow 없이 Paging3의 다음 페이지 로드를 제어한 방법 ​ 발표 대상 Jetpack Compose 기반 복잡한 인터렉션을 포함한 UI 개발에 관심 있는 Android 개발자 Jetpack Compose 관련 성능, 설계, 이슈에 대해 관심 있는 Android 개발자 복잡한 UI 를 AI 를 활용해 만들고 싶은 개발자 ​ 목차 ​ 문제의 UI: LazyRow로 만들 수 없었던 카드 덱 왜 LazyRow가 아닌가: 배치·스크롤·보이는 것만 컴포즈, 세 가지 약속 카드 덱의 동작 원리: Float 하나로 모든 카드를 움직이는 구조 이슈 ① 리컴포지션 0으로 매 프레임 움직이기 이슈 ② 3D로 기울인 UI의 터치 판정 이슈 ③ LazyRow 없이 Paging3 다루기 AI와 함께 만들기: 빨라진 것, 그리고 안 됐던 것 ​ ◎ NAVER Engineering Day란? ​ NAVER에서는 사내 개발 경험과 기술 트렌드를 교류를 할 수 있는 프로그램이 많이 있습니다. 그중 이제는 매회 평균 100개 이상의 발표가 이루어지는 NAVER Engineering Day를 빼놓을 수 없는데요. 2016년부터 시작된 ENGINEERING DAY는 실무에서의 기술 개발 경험과 새로운 기술과 플랫폼 도입 시 유용하게 활용될 수 있는 팁 등을 공유하며 서로 배우고 성장하는 네이버의 대표적인 사내 개발자 행사입니다.( 관련 포스팅 보기 ) 올해 진행된 NAVER Engineering Day의 일부 세션을 공개합니다. ​ [동영상 제공 채널 안내] 네이버 TV 서비스 종료로 인해 기존 네이버 TV 채널을 클립( @devrel_d2 )으로 이동하였습니다. 앞으로도 많은 관심과 팔로우 부탁드리겠습니다.

title: 목적마다, 상품마다 늘던 모델을 하나로: 금융 도메인에 멀티태스크 학습 적용하기
abstract: 회사가 커지면 서비스가 늘고, 서비스마다 끌어올리고 싶은 목표도 늘어납니다. "이 유저가 다음 달에 특정 상품을 신청할까", "이 유저가 어떤 상품에서 어떤 결과를 받고, 그때 조건은 어떻게 될까" 같은 질문이 하나씩 생길 때마다 모델을 하나씩 만들다 보면, 과제마다 · 상품마다 트리 모델이 계속 늘어 금세 수십~수백 개가 됩니다. 게다가 그 모델들은 대부분 매일 돌아야 해서, 배포 · 모니터링 · 재학습 · 유지보수 같은 운영 부담이 모델 수만큼 눈덩이처럼 불어나요. 어느새 ML 엔지니어(MLE)가 정작 판단에 써야 할 시간을 반복적인 모델 양산과 운영에 빼앗기게 됩니다. 모델을 잘 만드는 것만큼, 많은 모델을 효율적으로 관리하는 것이 중요해지는 이유예요. 토스의 서비스에서도 두 곳에서 실제로 그랬습니다. 하나는 마케팅 유입 입니다. 새 마케팅 목적이 생길 때마다 타겟팅에 쓸 예측 모델이 필요했고, 그때마다 트리 모델이 하나씩 늘었어요. 다른 하나는 상품 입니다. 상품마다 여러 가지 예측이 필요한데, 상품마다 트리 모델을 따로 두다 보니 모델이 수백 개로 불어났습니다. 지난 글(TASTE, 토스의 추천 파운데이션 플랫폼) 에서는 여러 행동을 함께 학습해 얻은 사용자 표현을 다른 서비스 모델에 전달하는 이야기를 했습니다. 멀티태스크 학습은 크게 두 가지로 쓸 수 있습니다. 하나는 여러 과제를 함께 학습하며 좋은 공유 표현을 만들고, 그 표현을 다른 모델에서 가져다 쓰는 것입니다. 다른 하나는 여러 과제의 예측값 자체를 하나의 모델로 잘 맞히는 것이에요. 지난 글이 앞의 경우에 무게를 두었다면, 이번 글은 뒤의 경우에 집중합니다. 같은 멀티태스크 학습 구조를 금융 도메인에 적용해, 목적마다 · 상품마다 늘던 예측 모델을 하나로 묶고 그 예측을 실제 마케팅과 서비스에 바로 쓰는 데 집중했습니다. 저희는 이 두 곳에서 늘어난 트리 모델들을 하나의 멀티태스크 모델(MTL, Multi-Task Learning)로 합치는 작업을 진행했습니다. 결론부터 말하면, 여러 목적의 유저 금융 행동 예측 : 목적마다 따로 두던 트리 모델들을, 수십 개 행동을 한 번에 예측하는 단 하나의 멀티태스크 모델로 합쳤습니다. 공유 인코더와 공유 전문가로 과제들이 서로의 데이터를 나눠 쓰도록 설계한 결과, 목적별 트리 모델 대비 평균 정밀도(AP, Average Precision)를 상대적으로 약 54% 끌어올렸고, 실제 마케팅에서도 불필요한 발송을 약 35% 줄이는 효율 개선으로 이어졌어요. 상품마다 따로 두던 과제들을 한 모델로 : 저희 경우에는 상품마다 서로 성격이 다른 세 가지 예측 과제가 필요했는데, 원래는 과제마다, 그리고 상품마다 트리 모델을 따로 두어 수백 개였습니다. 이를 세 과제를 함께 학습하는 MTL 하나로 묶고, 상품 정보를 입력으로 받아 새로 생기는 상품까지 모델을 새로 만들지 않고 한 번에 예측하게 했어요. 성능도 상품별 트리 모델보다 예측 오차(MAE)는 약 66~79% 줄고, AUC는 상대적으로 약 10% 올랐습니다. 상품이 몇 배로 늘어도 모델은 여전히 하나입니다. 여기서 핵심 메시지는 두 가지예요. 하나는 통합 — 과제마다, 상품마다 늘어나던 개별 모델을 하나의 모델로 묶었다 는 것. 다른 하나는 확장성 — 새 과제는 출력층을 더해 같은 모델에서 학습하고, 새 상품은 상품 정보를 입력으로 받기 때문에 모델을 새로 만들지 않고 같은 하나로 대응 한다는 것이에요. 규모를 키우면서 성능도 올리고, 질문이 계속 늘어나도 무리 없이 운영하고 개선할 수 있게 만드는 것이 목표였습니다. 이 글에서는 두 사례를 통해 멀티태스크 학습이 무엇을 해결해 줬는지, 그리고 무엇이 어려웠는지를 이야기하려 합니다. 개별 모델이 많아지면 생기는 문제 과제 하나에 모델 하나를 두는 방식은 처음에는 가장 단순합니다. 트리 모델은 빨리 만들 수 있고 성능도 괜찮아서, 새 목적이 생길 때마다 하나씩 더하기 좋습니다. 그런데 그렇게 모인 트리 모델이 수백 개가 되면, 비용도 과제 수 × 상품 수만큼 늘어요. 마케팅 목적이 늘 때마다, 상품이 늘 때마다 저희가 실제로 겪은 일입니다. 운영 비용 : 모델마다 학습 데이터 준비, 학습, 배포, 모니터링이 따로 있습니다. 모델이 수백 개면 파이프라인도 수백 개이고, 장애 지점도 그만큼 많습니다. 재학습 부담 : 데이터 분포는 계속 바뀌는데, 수백 개 모델을 모두 자주 다시 학습하기는 어렵습니다. 결국 한 번 만든 모델이 오래 고정되기 쉬워요. 새 데이터 · 새 실험의 비용 : 좋은 신호가 될 만한 데이터가 새로 생겨도, 효과가 있는지 확인하려면 모델마다 따로 다시 학습하고 실험해야 합니다. 모델이 일정 수를 넘어가면 이 실험을 바로 해 보기 어려워, 개선 아이디어가 있어도 미뤄지기 쉽습니다. 데이터가 적은 과제 : 드문 행동이나 정답이 드문 상품은 따로 학습하면 배울 것이 부족합니다. 새로 생긴 상품은 데이터가 쌓이고 개별 모델을 따로 만들기 전까지 쓸 수 있는 모델이 없어요. 멀티태스크 학습은 이 문제를 이렇게 풉니다. 비슷한 목적의 모델들을 하나로 묶고, 입력을 요약하는 공통 부분은 모든 과제가 함께 쓰고, 과제별 예측을 내는 마지막 부분만 과제마다 따로 둔다. 그러면 파이프라인은 하나가 되고, 재학습도 한 번이면 됩니다. 새 데이터를 넣거나 새 실험을 할 때도 모델 하나만 바꾸면 모든 과제에 한 번에 반영돼요. 이것은 저희만의 방향이 아닙니다. Meta도 광고 추천에서 수천 개의 도메인 × 목적 조합마다 따로 두던 모델을 비슷한 조합끼리 묶어 소수의 모델로 재설계했고, 품질 지표를 올리면서 인프라 용량도 약 20% 줄였다고 발표했습니다( Meta Lattice, Luo et al., KDD 2026 ). 다만 무작정 합치면 품질이 떨어져 "무엇끼리 묶을지"가 중요하다는 점도 함께 강조했어요. 두 사례에 공통으로 쓴 설계 저희가 만든 두 MTL 모델은 예측 대상이 전혀 다르지만, 뼈대는 같습니다. 둘 다 사내 ML 플랫폼 위에서 데이터 준비 → 학습 → 예측 → 평가가 돌아가고, 매일 다시 학습합니다. 플랫폼 자체는 지난 글 에서 소개했습니다. [그림 1] 두 사례에 공통으로 쓴 멀티태스크 뼈대. 과제가 늘어도 과제별 부분만 한 줄씩 추가됩니다. 공유 인코더 : 입력을 요약하는 부분은 과제와 상관없으니 한 번만 계산해 모든 과제가 함께 씁니다. PLE(Progressive Layered Extraction) : Tencent가 발표한 멀티태스크 구조입니다( RecSys 2020 ). 모든 과제가 함께 쓰는 공유 전문가와 과제별 전문가를 두고, 과제마다 게이트가 "어느 전문가를 얼마나 쓸지"를 정합니다. 과제별 게이트는 공유 전문가와 자기 전문가만 보기 때문에, 다른 과제가 끼어드는 간섭을 줄일 수 있어요. 과제별 출력층과 Loss : 마지막 출력층은 과제마다 따로 두고, Loss도 과제마다 계산해 더합니다. 라벨이 없는 과제는 Loss에서 뺀다 : 한 샘플 안에서도 어떤 과제는 정답이 있고 어떤 과제는 없습니다. 예를 들어 아래 사례 2 모델에서는 앞선 분류 과제의 정답이 '아니오'이면, 뒤따르는 두 수치 과제는 정답 자체가 없습니다. 그렇다고 이 샘플을 빼 버리면 분류 과제는 '아니오'인 경우를 배우지 못해요. 그래서 샘플은 그대로 두고, 정답이 없는 수치 과제의 Loss만 계산에서 뺐습니다. 과제마다 Loss의 균형을 맞춘다 : 단위와 분포가 다른 수치 과제는 타깃을 표준화해 과제 간 Loss 크기를 맞추고, 양성이 드문 분류 과제는 양성 가중치로 양성과 음성의 균형을 맞췄습니다. 이 뼈대 덕분에, 트리 모델 수백 개로는 얻기 어려웠던 두 가지 이점이 생겼습니다. 데이터가 적은 과제가 큰 과제에서 배운다 : 공유 인코더와 공유 전문가는 모든 과제의 데이터로 학습됩니다. 그래서 정답이 드문 과제도 비슷한 과제와 함께 학습됩니다. 따로 학습하면 데이터가 모자라 배우기 어려운 과제가, 묶이면서 출발점을 얻는 셈이에요. 표 밖의 입력을 쓸 수 있다 : 트리 모델의 입력은 고정 길이 표 한 줄이라, 시간 순서가 있는 정보를 쓰려면 사람이 집계 피처로 펴서 넣어야 합니다. 신경망 기반 MTL은 시간 순서가 있는 기록, 상

title: Why Can’t My Running Pods Be Reached? Our Journey to kube-proxy nftables Mode
abstract: Hi, I’m Karin, and I’m on the Cluster squad within SRE at Karrot. Our team designs and runs the Kubernetes platform that every service at Karrot runs on. We take responsibility for everything that keeps our clusters observable and reliable, from monitoring infrastructure all the way to the service mesh and security, along with the policies and roadmaps that keep it all maintainable. In this post, I’ll share how we migrated kube-proxy from iptables mode to nftables mode. kube-proxy runs on every node in a Kubernetes cluster and programs network rules into the Linux kernel so that traffic sent to a Service reaches the actual Pods. For years, our clusters ran kube-proxy in iptables mode to provide this core feature. Below, I’ll walk through how we moved to nftables, its more efficient successor, and what we learned along the way. 1. kube-proxy latency was hurting service reliability In Kubernetes, nodes come and go and Pods spin up all the time. That’s just how it works. But when a Pod lands on a fresh node and the app starts up, is it actually ready to talk to other services? kube-proxy manages the network rules (just “rules” from here on) on each node that let traffic headed for a Service reach the actual Pods . On a new node, if an application starts up while those rules are still being prepared, its DNS lookups and calls to other services can fail. kube-proxy rule sync lag had been creeping up for a while. We’d been watching the metrics since 2024, and latency was noticeably higher in our production cluster in the Korea region, the largest of all the regions we serve. But we judged it wasn’t serious enough to cause operational problems, and in practice, it never actually turned into an incident. Then, in the first half of this year, we made a big change: we adopted Karpenter. Now that we could scale out nodes quickly, we stopped using the Overprovisioner that used to keep spare nodes ready for Pods. As a result, Pods were landing on freshly created nodes much more often, which also raised the odds that an application would try to talk to something before rule sync had finished. Soon after, we started getting reports like the ones below, and most of them boiled down to “my Pod can’t talk to anything.” Putting our kube-proxy metrics from 2024 and 2026 side by side made it obvious how much heavier kube-proxy’s workload had gotten in just two years. Our service footprint and NAT rule count had grown noticeably, and Pods were being created and terminated far more often. Every time a Pod changes, the Service’s Endpoints (the IPs of the Pods that receive its traffic) change with it, so the number of changes kube-proxy had to apply grew right along with it. Rule sync latency got several times worse, and endpoint changes pending, which tracks Endpoint changes not yet reflected in the rules, went from occasional brief spikes to a steady backlog. Latency and endpoint changes pending in 2024 Latency and endpoint changes pending in 2026 network programming rate in 2024 network programming rate in 2026 In the first half of 2026, our service cluster had roughly 1,400 Services and 27,000 Pods, with about 80,000 iptables NAT rules. With Endpoints constantly churning from deploys and autoscaling, and nodes repeatedly being torn down and spun up, the initial rule sync on a new node sometimes took as long as 4 minutes and 20 seconds . (That’s over four minutes with no working Service or DNS traffic!) Once we confirmed this was actually affecting production, we had to fix it. After some intense discussion with the team, we decided to try switching kube-proxy from iptables mode to nftables mode. Here’s how the two modes differ. In iptables mode, kube-proxy creates rules for every Service and every Endpoint. When a packet comes in, it’s first matched against the Service rules one by one, top to bottom, to find the destination Service, and then against that Service’s Endpoint rules, again one by one, to pick a Pod. title: 파드는 떴는데 왜 통신이 안 될까? kube-proxy nftables 전환 여정
abstract: 안녕하세요, 당근 SRE팀 클러스터 파트에서 일하고 있는 Karin(카린)이에요. 클러스터 파트는 당근 내부의 모든 서비스가 운영되는 쿠버네티스 환경을 설계하고 관리해요. 쿠버네티스 환경의 가시성과 서비스 안정성을 확보하기 위해 모니터링 인프라부터 서비스 메시, 보안까지 여러 방면에서 정책과 로드맵을 설계하고 적용해요. 이 글에서는 kube-proxy를 iptables 모드에서 nftables 모드로 전환한 이야기를 해보려고 해요. kube-proxy는 쿠버네티스의 모든 노드에서 동작하면서, Service로 들어온 트래픽이 실제 Pod로 전달되도록 리눅스 커널에 네트워크 규칙을 설정하는 컴포넌트예요. 이 규칙을 관리하는 방식으로 오랫동안 iptables를 써왔는데, 이를 더 효율적인 후속 도구인 nftables로 바꾼 과정과 그 과정에서 배운 점을 공유하려고 해요. 1. kube-proxy latency가 서비스 안정성에 영향을 미쳤어요 쿠버네티스에서 노드가 새로 생기고 Pod가 뜨는 것은 매우 자연스러운 일이죠. 그런데 새 노드에 Pod가 스케줄링되고 애플리케이션이 시작되었다고 해서, 다른 서비스와 통신할 준비도 모두 끝난 걸까요? kube-proxy는 각 노드에서 Service로 향하는 트래픽이 실제 Pod에 도달할 수 있게 네트워크 규칙(이하 ‘규칙’)을 관리 하는데요, 새 노드에서는 이 규칙을 준비하는 동안 애플리케이션이 먼저 시작하면 DNS 조회나 다른 서비스와의 통신에 실패할 수 있어요. kube-proxy의 규칙 동기화가 느려지고 있다는 것은 예전부터 알고 있었어요. 2024년부터 지표를 지켜보니, 다른 리전보다 규모가 큰 한국 프로덕션에서 유독 지연이 높았거든요. 그러나 운영상 문제가 될 정도는 아니라고 판단했고, 실제로도 이슈로 이어진 적은 없었어요. 하지만 올해 상반기에 Karpenter를 도입하는 큰 변화가 있었어요. 노드를 빠르게 scale-out할 수 있게 되면서 Pod가 사용할 노드를 미리 준비하던 Overprovisioner를 더 이상 사용하지 않게 됐어요. 그 결과 새로 생성된 노드에 Pod가 곧바로 스케줄링되는 상황을 더 자주 마주했어요. 규칙 동기화가 끝나기 전에 애플리케이션이 통신을 시도할 가능성도 커진 거죠. 이후에 아래와 같은 문의가 들어오기 시작했고, 대부분은 ‘Pod가 통신이 안 된다’라는 제보였어요. 2024년과 2026년의 kube-proxy 지표를 나란히 놓고 보니, 2년 사이 kube-proxy의 부담이 크게 늘어난 걸 뚜렷하게 확인할 수 있었어요. 서비스 규모와 NAT 규칙 수가 눈에 띄게 늘었고, Pod가 생성되고 종료되는 일도 잦아졌어요. Pod가 바뀔 때마다 Service의 목적지를 나타내는 Endpoint, 즉 트래픽을 받을 Pod의 IP도 함께 바뀌기 때문에 kube-proxy가 반영해야 할 변경도 그만큼 늘어났어요. 그 결과 규칙 동기화 지연은 이전보다 몇 배 커졌고, 아직 규칙에 반영되지 못한 Endpoint 변경을 나타내는 endpoint changes pending 지표도 과거에는 잠깐씩 튀던 값이 지속적으로 쌓이는 모습으로 바뀌었어요. 2024년의 latency와 endpoint changes pending 2026년의 latency와 endpoint changes pending 2024년의 network programming rate 2026년의 network programming rate 2026년 상반기 당시 서비스 클러스터에는 약 1,400개의 Service와 27,000개의 Pod가 있었고, iptables의 NAT 규칙은 약 80,000개에 달했어요. 배포와 오토스케일링으로 Endpoint가 계속 바뀌는 가운데, 노드가 반복적으로 종료되고 생성될 때는 첫 규칙 동기화에 최대 4분 20초 가 걸리기도 했어요. 4분 넘게 Service와 DNS 통신이 안 되는 상태였던 거예요! 실제 서비스 운영에 영향을 주는 문제라는 것을 확인했기 때문에 이 문제를 해결해야 했어요. 팀원들과 개선 방안을 치열하게 의논한 결과 iptables 모드에서 nftables 모드로 전환해 보기로 했어요. 두 모드의 차이점은 다음과 같아요. iptables 모드에서 kube-proxy는 Service마다, 그리고 Endpoint마다 규칙을 만들어요. 패킷이 들어오면 먼저 Service 규칙을 위에서부터 차례로 비교해 목적지 Service를 찾고, 다시 그 Service의 Endpoint 규칙을 차례로 비교해 보낼 Pod를 골라요. 두 단계 모두 순차 비교라서 Service가 많을수록, 그리고 Service 하나에 붙은 Endpoint가 많을수록 비교할 규칙이 늘어나 조회 비용이 O(N)이에요. 더 큰 문제는 규칙을 갱신할 때예요. 전체 규칙 수는 Service와 Endpoint 수에 비례하고, 규칙이 많을수록 갱신 시간도 길어져요. 그런데 Endpoint는 Pod가 변경될 때 함께 바뀌어서 갱신이 자주 일어나다 보니, 반영하지 못한 변경이 점점 쌓였어요. 특히 kube-proxy가 시작한 직후에는 전체 규칙을 새로 쓰는 full sync를 하는데, 규모가 커진 당근 클러스터에서는 이 시간이 4분을 넘기도 했어요. nftables 모드는 Service를 찾는 단계와 Endpoint를 고르는 단계를 모두 map 기반으로 처리해요. 목적지 IP . 프로토콜 . 포트를 키로 map을 조회해서 해당 Service로 바로 이동하고, Endpoint도 목록을 하나씩 훑지 않고 map에서 바로 골라요. 그래서 Service나 Endpoint가 늘어나도 조회 비용은 O(1)에 가깝게 유지돼요. 갱신할 때도 지난 동기화 이후 바뀐 Service와 Endpoint만 반영하므로, 비용이 전체 규모가 아니라 변경량에 비례해요. Endpoint가 많고 자주 바뀌는 환경일수록 이 차이가 크게 드러나요. 하지만 모드를 변경하기 전에, 몇 가지 질문이 있었어요. 무엇이 규칙 동기화를 느리게 만들고 있었을까요? Service와 Endpoint가 많아서일까요? 변경이 자주 발생해서일까요? nftables로 바꾸면 얼마나 개선될까요? nftables 모드로 ‘안전하게’ 전환할 수 있을까요? 이 질문에 답하기 위해, 테스트 클러스터에서 조건을 바꿔가며 latency를 측정하고 iptables와 nftables를 비교하는 실험을 해보기로 했어요. 첫 동기화 시간을 20초 이내로 줄여야 한다고 판단했고, 실험으로 이를 검증하고자 했어요. 2. 실험의 네 가지 목표 실험을 시작하기 전에, 이 프로젝트에서 무엇을 확인할지 네 가지로 정리했어요. 1. 조건에 따른 규칙 동기화 지연 시간 확인 Service와 Endpoint가 많은 것과, 그 Endpoint가 자주 바뀌는 것은 다른 조건이겠죠? 같은 수의 Pod를 배포하더라도 조금씩 교체할 때와 한꺼번에 교체할 때의 영향이 다를 수 있고요. 규모, 변경 빈도, 배포 패턴을 나눠서 각각 latency에 어떤 영향을 주는지 측정해보기로 했어요. 2. 같은 조건에서 iptables와 nftables를 비교 nftables의 성능이 좋다고 알려져 있어도, 당근의 운영 환경에서 얼마나 개선될지는 직접 확인하고 싶었어요. 테스트 클러스터에서 같은 부하를 만들어 성능을 비교하기로 했어요. 3. 프로덕션에 안전하게 적용할 수 있는지 확인 테스트에서 빨라졌다고 바로 전환할 수는 없겠죠? 당근에서 사용하는 VPC CNI, Istio 등의 addon 구성과 충돌 없이 동작하는지, 알려진 이슈 중 우리 환경에 해당하는 것은 없는지 살펴봐야 했어요. 4. kube-proxy 버전을 유지할지, 함께 업그레이드할지 당시 EKS는 v1.34이지만, kube-proxy는 v1.34에서 이슈( https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/135323 )가 발견되어 v1.31을 유지하고 있었어요. v1.31에서도 nftables 모드를 사용할 수 있었기 때문에, 모드만 변경하는 방법과 v1.34로 올리면서 변경하는 방법을 모두 검토했어요. 버전마다 성능과 알려진 이슈가 다를 수 있으니, 개선 폭과 운영 위험을 함께 비교해 결정하고자 했어요. 3. 먼저, 무엇을 측정

title: Field Life: Particle Life as Interacting Chemical Fields
abstract: Field Life is a cellular automaton inspired by the interaction dynamics of Particle Life. In Particle Life, each particle has a colour, and an interaction matrix sets how strongly each colour attracts or repels each other colour. In Field Life, each colour is a channel of the automaton, and each cell holds a concentration of every colour. One step of the rule has three parts. Each colour is convolved with a ring-shaped kernel, which measures how much of that colour surrounds a cell. The interaction matrix combines these measurements into an attraction for each colour. The mass of each colour then moves toward higher attraction, in a way that conserves mass. A random matrix and a random initial state are usually enough to produce moving structure: bodies that glide, bodies that shed diffuse clouds, and gliders that break up into smaller gliders. We sample rules at random, keep the rules that move and form structure, and describe the patterns that appear: colours that sort into regions, colours that form stripes, and gliders, compact bodies that travel across the grid. The simulation and 120 saved rules, which we call worlds, are released.

title: E(n)-Equivariant Spherical Decision Surfaces
abstract: We present a constructive derivation of exactly E(n)-equivariant spherical decision surfaces by extending prior O(n)-equivariant hypersphere neurons to include translations. To achieve this, we present a decomposition of the features of the O(n)-equivariant neurons and provide explicit representations for translation and E(n)-transformations to fulfil the respective equivariance constraints. The resulting decision surfaces are exactly E(n)-equivariant without input centring or explicit pairwise differences, and admit explicit closed-form matrix representations. In addition, we numerically verify the correctness of the derivations and perform a downstream check of the resulting geometric primitives.

title: Accuracy of Noise Ceiling Estimators for Brain Scores
abstract: The internal activations of modern machine learning models align surprisingly well with the activities recorded in real brains. In the last five years, the alignment between encoding models and brain activities, often called brain scores, has steadily increased. Because brain recordings are noisy, there exists an upper bound to the brain scores that any model can achieve. This bound, called the noise ceiling, is crucial for two reasons: it determines whether further improvements in model performance are possible, and it enables meaningful comparisons of brain scores across benchmarks. The field has developed multiple approaches to estimate noise ceilings, but the statistical properties of existing estimators remain poorly understood, leaving it unclear in which experimental settings they provide reliable estimates. Here, we introduce a unified mathematical framework for brain recordings, use it to derive closed-form expressions for four commonly used noise ceiling estimators, and provide theoretical predictions for the behavior of each estimator. We validate the theoretical predictions with simulations that we compare to noise ceiling estimates in existing fMRI and EEG datasets. We find that the existing methods underestimate the true noise ceiling in different settings. We conclude with recommendations for best practice in different situations.

title: Measuring Layer-wise Intrinsic Dimensionality of FFNs in LLMs via PCA
abstract: Modern large language models (LLMs) keep the feed-forward network (FFN) intermediate width identical across every layer, a convention inherited from the original Transformer. Yet mechanistic work suggests layers at different depths do qualitatively different work, raising a natural question: are their capacity demands also non-uniform, and if so, can a fixed parameter budget be allocated more wisely than uniformly? To probe this, we apply principal component analysis (PCA) to the input of each FFN down-projection and measure, for every layer, its intrinsic dimensionality as the smallest number of principal components needed to reconstruct the activation up to a fixed cosine similarity. Scanning 58 open-weight LLMs spanning 14 families and 70M to 72B parameters, we find a recurring middle-heavy profile in which middle layers carry higher intrinsic dimensionality than edge layers; the profile is robust to the calibration corpus, even across English and Chinese, and is largely preserved through post-training fine-tuning.
